b: Hypersensitivity reactions are exaggerated or inappropriate immune responses that cause tissue damage. They are classified into four main types:

Type I (Immediate) Hypersensitivity is IgE mediated . It involves the rapid degranulation of mast cells upon re-exposure to an allergen, leading to the release of inflammatory mediators. Examples include anaphylaxis and asthma .

Type II (Cytotoxic) Hypersensitivity is mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies that bind to antigens on cell surfaces. This binding can lead to cell destruction through complement activation or antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC

qs.q: A positive tuberculin skin test, with a firm 15 mm diameter dark red area of induration on the forearm, appears 60 hours after injection of purified protein derivative (PPD). This finding is most likely a consequence of which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
qs.e: * The tuberculin skin test relies on an intact cell-mediated immune response. It is positive with prior mycobacterial exposure, so memory T cells are present and can be reactivated.

qs.q: A positive tuberculin skin test shows 15 mm of firm dark red induration at 60 hours after PPD injection. Most likely type of hypersensitivity reaction?
qs.e: Delayed reaction peaking at 48–72 hours + induration (not just redness) + requires prior sensitization = type IV (cell-mediated/delayed-type) hypersensitivity, mediated by memory T lymphocytes responding to mycobacterial antigens.

qs.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by IgE antibodies and involves mast cell degranulation and histamine release?
qs.e: Type I hypersensitivity (immediate hypersensitivity) is mediated by IgE antibodies binding to mast cells and basophils, leading to rapid degranulation upon re-exposure to the allergen and release of inflammatory mediators like histamine.

qs.q: Which immunoglobulin is associated with immediate hypersensitivity reactions and defense against parasitic infections, primarily by binding to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils?
qs.e: IgE antibodies are strongly associated with allergic reactions (Type I hypersensitivity) and play a role in immunity against parasites. They bind with high affinity to Fc receptors (FcεRI) on mast cells and basophils.

ai.title: Hypersensitivity Reactions
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Exaggerated immune responses that damage tissue. Clinicians must identify type, severity and trigger, then stop the inciting agent and give appropriate supportive care.

sections.p: Hypersensitivity reactions are immune‐mediated tissue injuries classified into four types (I–IV). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history, examination and selective tests.
b: Type I: IgE‑mediated, immediate; Type II: antibody‑mediated cytotoxic; Type III: immune‑complex; Type IV: T‑cell mediated delayed

sections.p: Severity is graded by the extent of systemic involvement and risk of death. The Brighton Collaboration criteria for anaphylaxis are useful in low‑resource settings.
b: Mild: localized urticaria or pruritus; Moderate: bronchospasm, hypotension, or facial swelling; Severe: anaphylaxis with shock, respiratory arrest or multi‑organ failure

sections.p: In East Africa, common triggers include antimalarials, cotrimoxazole, antiretrovirals, herbal remedies, and infections such as malaria, TB and schistosomiasis.
b: Drug reactions (cotrimoxazole, antimalarials, antiretrovirals); infections (malaria, TB, schistosomiasis); herbal preparations; food allergens; insect bites

sections.p: Presentation depends on type. Type I is rapid, with urticaria, angioedema and anaphylaxis. Type II shows cytopenias or hemolysis. Type III presents with fever, arthralgia, and glomerulonephritis. Type IV is delayed skin reaction or granulomatous disease.
b: Type I: hives, wheeze, hypotension within minutes; Type II: pallor, jaundice, anemia; Type III: fever, rash, arthralgia, renal dysfunction; Type IV: erythema, induration, fever after 24–72h

sections.p: Use the simplest tests that answer a specific question. When unavailable, clinical judgment prevails.

t.b: Detects IgE to specific allergens; positive if wheal >3mm after 15min – useful for Type I
Identifies eosinophilia (Type I), anemia or thrombocytopenia (Type II), or leukocytosis (Type III/IV) – abnormal values guide urgency
Elevated in IgE‑mediated reactions – supports diagnosis when skin testing is not possible
Low in immune‑complex disease – suggests Type III
Positive indicates cytotoxic antibody mediated injury – Type II

sections.p: Early recognition of life‑threatening features is vital. Complications include shock, organ failure, and delayed autoimmune sequelae.
b: Hypotension <90/60 mmHg; tachycardia >120/min; wheeze or stridor; altered mental status; oliguria; rash with systemic spread; severe cytopenias

sections.p: Stop the offending agent, then give organ‑specific supportive care. Drug choice is guided by safety and availability.
b: Antihistamine (H1 blocker) – blocks histamine release; corticosteroid – reduces inflammation and prevents biphasic reaction; epinephrine – first‑line for anaphylaxis; IV fluids – treat hypotension; oxygen – for respiratory compromise

t.b: Crystalloid 20ml/kg bolus to restore preload in shock

sections.p: Patients should receive education on avoidance, carry emergency medication, and have a written action plan.
b: Avoid known trigger; use alternative drugs; carry epinephrine auto‑injector; document reaction in medical record; refer to allergy clinic if available

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hypersensitivity but have different pathophysiology.
b: Drug toxicity (e.g., paracetamol overdose); sepsis; viral exanthem; urticarial vasculitis; autoimmune hemolytic anemia

sections.p: Some investigations may be falsely normal early or due to concurrent disease.
b: IgE may be normal in non‑IgE mediated reactions; eosinophilia may be absent in severe anaphylaxis; complement may be normal in early immune‑complex disease

whenToSeekHelp: Anaphylaxis with hypotension, wheeze, or altered consciousness; severe cytopenias or hemolysis; sudden renal failure; unexplained shock

faq.q: Why is cotrimoxazole contraindicated in severe hypersensitivity?
faq.a: It can trigger life‑threatening anaphylaxis and severe cutaneous reactions; stopping it immediately is mandatory.

faq.q: Can a patient with a mild urticarial reaction develop anaphylaxis later?
faq.a: Yes, biphasic reactions occur; monitor for at least 4–6 hours after resolution.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient on cotrimoxazole develops fever, rash and hemolysis – what is the likely type and first step? — Type II cytotoxic; stop cotrimoxazole immediately and give supportive care.
A child presents with wheeze and hypotension 10 minutes after a bee sting – what is the immediate management? — Intramuscular epinephrine, oxygen, IV fluids.
A patient with chronic urticaria has no response to antihistamines; what is the next diagnostic step? — Skin prick testing or serum IgE if available.
A 45‑year‑old woman develops fever, arthralgia and a palpable purpura 48h after starting a new antibiotic – what is the most likely type? — Type III immune complex; check complement levels.
A patient with suspected drug reaction has eosinophilia and acute kidney injury – what is the most probable mechanism? — Type II cytotoxic or Type III; consider drug‑induced lupus.

A rural clinician has no access to skin testing; a patient has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin – what should the clinician do? — Avoid penicillin, use alternative antibiotics, and provide an epinephrine auto‑injector.

A patient with a history of severe allergic reaction to a herbal remedy presents with facial swelling – what is the most appropriate first action? — Stop the herb, give antihistamine and consider epinephrine if airway compromise.
